# Gold Mining Tycoon: Design Document

**Status:** the owner's rulings of 2026-10-05 are applied (§0 records them; no question is open). The design covers every system through Phase 6, nothing is implemented yet, and it awaits the owner's go-ahead for Phase 0.

**Companion files:**
- [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md): how we build.
- [`BALANCE.md`](BALANCE.md): economic targets and the simulator checks.
- [`docs/BRIEF.md`](docs/BRIEF.md): the original brief, verbatim.

## How to read this document

- **§0 records the owner's rulings** of 2026-10-05: what was asked, what was decided, and which sections and decisions changed. Any new question that becomes expensive to reverse is added there before it is decided.
- **"The game in brief"** comes next: a two-page tour of how the game plays, with the headline numbers.
- **Every system section opens with an *At a glance* box.** Read only those for a 20-minute tour, then go deeper where you care.
- **Every system section (§1, §3–§14) has the same layout:** rules, formulas, data shapes, worked examples, player actions, weekly resolution, interfaces, phase plan, tuning constants, balance levers, tests, decisions, open questions, sources. §2, the technical contract, keeps rules, data shapes, phase plan, tuning, tests, decisions and open questions.
- **Ownership:** each concept has one owning section, and other sections refer to it rather than redefine it. §2 is the technical contract: engine API, determinism, units, IDs, RNG streams, the weekly pipeline, saves, and the simulator and its bot catalog.
- **Tuning constants** are written `namespace.key` with a default value. Those names are the keys in `src/data/tuning/`, so any number can be found and changed without touching logic. Tags after a number give its source: `[V]` checked against a cited source, `[M]` or `[U]` model knowledge not yet verified, and `R1`–`R5` the research sheets in [`docs/research/`](docs/research/README.md).
- **Units:**
  - Money is USD, stored as integer cents.
  - Gold is troy ounces, always labeled *raw* (as weighed) or *fine* (pure gold content).
  - Volume is bank cubic yards (bcy); grade is raw oz per bcy; area is acres.
  - The §14 hard-rock track uses short tons and oz/ton.
- **Phases:** P0–P6 in each phase plan match the build phases in `CLAUDE.md`.
- **Decisions:** §15 indexes every decision (`D-<section>.<n>`). Each section keeps its own full list with rationale.

### Smaller calls

The owner confirmed every call below on 2026-10-05 except item 3, which the rulings changed; item 24 was added with the rulings.

1. **Saves across phases:** a save from phase N loads in phase N+1, so every schema change from P1 on ships with a migration and a fixture. P0 saves are not supported (OQ-2.1; D-2.34).
2. **Test before you buy:** a paid, exclusive inspection period on a listing. It lasts 2–8 weeks and costs 0.7% of the ask per week (×1.5 for notice-tier work), credited if you buy. Fixed price in P2, negotiable from P5 (OQ-4.1; D-4.39, D-5.44).
3. **Agencies: real names** (owner ruling 2026-10-05, replacing the fictional analogs). Districts are fictional but located in Alaska, Nevada and Yukon; the real agencies administer them through §6's agency map; a one-line in-game disclaimer says the rules are simplified game mechanics, not legal or regulatory advice; agency text never shows seals, letterhead or real officials (OQ-6.1; D-6.1, D-6.53–D-6.57, D-13.67).
4. **Injuries at research rates:** rare for careful small crews, about 0.06 lost-time injuries per season. Doubling them is one key plus a re-tune of WC and §12 incidents (OQ-8.1; D-8.17).
5. **Refinery timing:** the refinery, metal accounts and forwards stay in P5 (moving them to P4 would cost about a week of extra P4 work). The P4 revolver uses equipment and seasonal over-advance only (OQ-10.1; D-10.27, D-11.50).
6. **Gold has a slightly positive real drift:** median about +10% real over 10 years, in line with history (OQ-10.2; D-10.19, D-10.29).
7. **Desktop only:** mouse and keyboard, full layout from 1280 px, graceful down to 1024 px, no touch (OQ-13.1; D-13.27).
8. **Hard rock in scoring:** on in the sandbox, off in goal scenarios unless they name it, and off when the brief's first-two-seasons targets are measured (OQ-14.2; D-14.33).
9. **The own-mill path includes cyanide (CIL)** in P6e, with its permits and bonds (OQ-14.3).
10. **Starting cash raised after the preflight model.**
    - Bootstrapper: $400k company cash.
    - Inheritor: $300k company cash (BALANCE R-3, approved), plus two blocks the family stripped in its last season, an estate note paid June–November, and a ripper.
    - Difficulty cash multipliers narrowed to 1.25 / 1.0 / 0.85 (D-1.42, D-1.43, D-1.54).
11. **Calendar:** a fixed 52-week year with no leap days, starting in January; year 1 is shown as 2027 (D-1.1; `game.startCalendarYear`, §1.3).
12. **Federal claim fees have no grace period at any difficulty.** Auto-pay for claim fees defaults on at every difficulty. Permit and bond auto-pay default off on standard and hard (D-6.16).
13. **Gold is sold to keep cash at or above $0.** New games start with this standing order (`keepCashAbove`, which you can switch off), so payroll is not missed while gold sits in camp (D-10.31).
14. **Mercy in distress:** from P5, outside bad events are 0.6 times as likely on standard (0.4 on easy, 0.8 on hard) while the company is at distress stage 3 or worse (missed payroll), and in a reorganization case from the filing until the plan is confirmed; plan years after confirmation get no mercy unless a stage-3 condition returns (D-12.6, D-12.49).
15. **The equity investor can end the run.** From P4, two hostile check-ins in a row plus an unpaid redemption demand means ouster; during a reorganization case no redemption demand is made, and an equity holder's conversion motion makes one missed plan payment convert the case (D-1.17, D-1.58).
16. **The owner cannot die.** A fatal roll on the owner becomes a serious injury (D-8.21).
17. **Competitor limits:** competitors cannot buy your company or end your run, never reorganize, propose no plan in your case, and none mine hard rock in P6 (D-12.23, D-12.49, D-12.50, D-14.22).
18. **Entity types:** no S-corp election. The sole proprietor gets a real early-credit edge: for the first 104 weeks the owner's own credit file stands in for the company's (D-1.14, D-1.36).
19. **BLM, the federal land agency, never fines.** It uses orders, standing and bonds; the state and water agencies and MSHA, the federal mine-safety agency, do fine (D-6.21).
20. **Undo is limited.** Only within the current week, and never for an action that drew a random number, revealed information or committed to a counterparty (D-2.22, D-13.11).
21. **Contained gold and losses are never shown.** You see the scale weight and a reconciliation against your estimate (D-13.7).
22. **Leasing your own claims to AI operators** is out of scope through P6 (D-5.26).
23. **The gold-price path is fixed by the seed.** The player cannot move the price (D-10.20).
24. **Each plant line rolls its own dice.** The `ops-skim`, `ops-freeze` and `ops-audit` streams take `lineId` as their last key part, so each line rolls its own skim, frost damage and tailings audit and adding a line never shifts another line's draws (D-7.50). It changes RNG key shapes, which CLAUDE.md treats as expensive, but no code, saves or golden replays exist yet, so it was accepted as a decision on 2026-10-05.

## The game in brief

**You are the Owner of a small placer gold mining company.** One turn is one week. The game starts in January of year 1, shown as 2027, with the whole off-season ahead. You never touch a machine. You decide what ground to buy or lease and how hard to test it, what to permit, what iron to buy, rent or finance, whom to hire and how to pay them, how to fund the season, and when and where to sell the gold. The weekly simulation resolves what the crew moved and washed, what the plant recovered, what broke, what it all cost, and what the gold was worth. The screens are dense business software in a frontier mining theme (earth tones, Daylight and Lamplight modes, a period face for titles only), and every number opens its own calculation (§2.8, §13.13, §13.20).

### The year

| When | What happens | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Jan–Apr** (north) | Off-season. Buy or lease ground; test it (pans, records, test pits, drilling on frozen ground); file permits; line up money; buy iron at auction or from dealers; hire for spring; move heavy iron in on the winter trail while it is open. | §4 §5 §6 §9 §11 |
| **Breakup**, about week 18–20 | Roads close for a few weeks, the ground starts to thaw, and the crew arrives. Cash outflows peak while no gold has come in yet. | §1.4 §7.12 §11.15 |
| **Season**, about 22 weeks (19–25) | Strip, mine, haul and wash. Recovery depends on matching the plant to the gold's particle size; push the plant too hard and fine gold goes out with the tailings. Clean up every week or two and weigh raw gold. Royalties come off the top. Sell, hold or ship to a refinery. Strip ahead for next year, because frozen muck thaws slowly. | §7 §8 §10 |
| **Freeze-up**, about week 42 | Winterize. Lay off or retain the crew. The first full year of numbers arrives. | §7.12 §8 |
| **Winter** | Rebuild machines in the shop. Debt payments and fees run all year, and the September 1 claim fee and December filings are real deadlines. Plan the next season. | §6.9 §9 §11 |

Arid districts invert the calendar. They can be worked most of the year, but water is the limit (wells, recycling, trucked water), summer brings heat and fire closures, and the monsoon brings flash floods.

**Fictional places, real regulators.** The districts are fictional but sit in interior Alaska, Nevada and (from P6) Alaska state land and Yukon, run by the real agencies: BLM, MSHA, the Corps of Engineers, Alaska DNR, DEC and ADF&G, Nevada NDEP and NDWR, and in Yukon EMR, YESAB, the Yukon Water Board and DFO. A disclaimer says the rules are simplified game mechanics, not legal or regulatory advice (§6.1).

### Starts and edges

| Start | Company cash / personal cash / owner credit | What comes with it |
|---|---|---|
| **Bootstrapper** | $400k / $120k / 760 | Nothing else. Full control and good credit. |
| **Backed (equity)** | $1.5M / $50k / 720 | An investor puts in $1.3M for 40%, with an 8% preferred return, a board seat and approval rights; from P4, hostile check-ins and an unpaid redemption demand end the run (§1.8.1). |
| **Backed (royalty)** | $1.1M / $50k / 720 | An investor puts in $0.9M for 10% of every fine ounce until 2× is repaid, then 3% for life. |
| **Inheritor** | $300k / $40k / 680 | Three family claims (60 acres) of unknown quality, an optimistic family ledger, a worn fleet with a ripper (resale about $152k), two blocks stripped last season, a $320k estate note paid June to November and, from P2, an under-bonded Plan of Operations. |

Each owner background gives one quantified edge, worth roughly one skilled hire:
- **Operator:** runs a claim as foreman at skill 85.
- **Mechanic:** skill-85 mechanic who inspects iron for free and adds 50 shop hours a week.
- **Geologist:** skill-75 geologist who catches seller fraud.
- **Banker:** lenders treat the company one credit tier higher.
- **Landman:** better negotiation and title diligence, and faster permits.

Entity type (sole proprietor, LLC or corporation) trades liability protection against cost, taxes and personal guarantees (§1.6).

### The heart of the game: you never know what is in the ground

Each claim is a grid of 1-acre blocks. Each block has hidden true geology:
- overburden and pay thickness;
- grade (raw oz per bank cubic yard), with a down-valley paystreak and rare rich pockets;
- the gold's particle size mix and fineness (0.70–0.92);
- permafrost, clay and boulders;
- whatever the old-timers already took.

Of the ground offered for sale, about **70% is uneconomic** once stripping is counted, about 22% is marginal, about 7% is good and about 1% is excellent (§3.7; the P0 full-generator run settles the exact shares, D-3.36). Sellers may be accurate, optimistic, cherry-picking or fraudulent (§3.10). The player buys evidence: every sample is a real random draw from the true ground with a nugget effect, so a pan of coarse-gold gravel is nearly worthless and a 10-yard pit is informative. A Bayesian estimator turns that evidence into per-block and per-claim **P10/P50/P90** ranges and a confidence class (§4). The end-of-run report reveals the truth.

### What a season is worth (preflight model, BALANCE §9)

The reference small northern operation is the owner plus 4–6 crew, a 30-t excavator, a D8-class dozer, a 966-class loader, a 30-t rock truck, a 75 bcy/hr trommel, two pumps, a generator and a camp. In an established season it washes **about 61,500 bcy at about 63 bcy/hr** (a minimal starter fleet manages about 36) and recovers **about 500 raw oz (≈ 430 fine, the anchor §1.8.1 and §7.20 use)**. The first season, on frozen ground with nothing stripped ahead, yields about 81% of that. Fuel and wages are **64–66% of site operating cost**. On a 0.012 oz/bcy claim the operating margin is **about $319k**, before royalties and debt service. Break-even pay grade is about **0.0113 oz/bcy** at a 3:1 stripping ratio on frozen ground, after royalty. A mature two-shift operation washes about 240 bcy/hr. A profitable northern year can still hit a cash low in May or June.

**Growing.** A company grows by adding claims, and the owner chooses how it scales (§7.2.1, §8.12, §9.8.6): from P3 a big claim can run a second or third plant line (more throughput for duplicated plant capital, shared water and more supervision); a crew of three or fewer can work without a foreman, saving a salary at some cost in efficiency and safety; and from P3 mechanics can be pooled across a district's road-access claims, trading response time and travel hours for fewer hires.

### How you lose, and how you fight it

Losing happens on a visible ladder of distress stages (§11.16; full from P4, while P1–P3 use a simpler insolvency counter, §1.14):

0. cash warning;
1. late vendors;
2. a missed loan payment;
3. **missed payroll** (morale collapses and wage claims follow);
4. default notices;
5. repossession of specific collateral;
6. forced sales;
7. bankruptcy, in two forms. A **liquidation** (Chapter 7) ends the run. From P4 an eligible company may instead file a Chapter 11 **Subchapter V reorganization** and keep playing: the stay holds lenders off while the owner proposes a 3–5-year plan paid from disposable income, which the court tests and creditors vote on. It costs fees, a credit crash, cash-on-delivery vendors, owner pay capped at living costs and a silver cap on any scenario medal; two missed plan payments mean liquidation (§11.16, §0.9).

At every rung there are counter-moves: sell gold, claims or iron; renegotiate; take emergency hard money; bring in a rescue partner on bad terms; inject personal cash; lay off crew; idle the operation. Entity type and personal guarantees decide how much of the owner's own money goes down with the company.

### Balance at a glance (BALANCE.md)

**Targets.** A careful player on standard survives two seasons as a going concern 60–70% of the time **and** avoids bankruptcy at least 75% of the time; both are gated, and a filing of either kind counts as a failure for its window (§0.3). A first-season profit is possible but not typical. Undercapitalized play on untested ground usually fails. No strategy dominates.

**Preflight results** (a reduced Python model, run before any engine exists; BALANCE §9):
- **P1 rules:** 68% of careful runs survive two seasons as a going concern (pooled over the four starts), 36% make a first-season profit, and 15% of undercapitalized runs survive.
- **Full rules** (a P5-like set with permits, a moving price, refinery sales and basic financing, standing in for P4–P6): survival 55%, still below the band, mainly because of permit waits; first-season profit 19%.
- **No bankruptcy:** pooled over the starts, careful runs avoid bankruptcy 85–93% of the time in every lever check, above the 75% floor (measured before reorganization existed).
- **Also off:** the careful bot dominates balanced and aggressive (O-04), cost per ounce is high for the Backed and Inheritor starts (O-14), the Inheritor trails on year-5 net worth (O-06 b), and difficulty is not yet ordered (O-05, gating in P6). BALANCE §9.5 holds the tuning plan, approved by the owner on 2026-10-05.

### What gets built when

| Phase | Adds |
|---|---|
| **P0** | Scaffold; deterministic engine core; world generator and estimator calibration; saves; simulator skeleton; the themed UI shell. |
| **P1** | Playable core loop: every entity, background and start; two federal districts (north and arid); buy or lease; the full estimator (pans, records, test pits; no drilling yet); the foreman rule and its small-crew exception; cash-bought equipment; hiring; full operations; flat gold price and local buyer; ledger and P&L. |
| **P2** | U.S. federal permitting in full under the real agencies, plus staking, the starter permitted lease, trenches and bulk samples, injuries and training. |
| **P3** | Equipment depth (wear, failures, shop, parts; certified, private, auction and rental markets), drilling, several plant lines per claim, district shop pools, and the equipment events. |
| **P4** | Finance depth (credit, every lender and product except gold loans, royalty and stream sales, covenants, the full distress ladder with reorganization, insurance, taxes, reports), investor check-ins and ouster, and the finance and labor events. |
| **P5** | Living market (gold price model and news, refinery, gold loans, hedging, the rest of the events, AI competitors, negotiation, claim auctions). |
| **P6** | Alaska-style and Yukon-style regimes, delegation depth (foremen and specialists who act on their own), JVs, scenarios and difficulty; then the optional hard-rock track (§14). |

Each phase ends playable, with tests green and a balance report against BALANCE.md; the build then stops for the owner's review before the next phase starts.

---

## 1. Vision, Pillars, and Game Structure

> **At a glance.** The player is the Owner of a small placer gold company. One turn is one week, on a fixed 52-week calendar that starts in week 1 (January) of year 1, displayed as 2027. Each district rolls its own breakup and freeze-up every year, so a northern operating window runs 19–25 weeks (typically 22). The player sees a forecast range for both dates that narrows as they approach. Weekly weather (temperature band, precipitation, stream flow, fire danger) feeds water supply, permafrost thaw, plant hours, fire restrictions, and event odds. Setup choices are real bets: entity type (liability shield vs cost and taxes), background (one quantified edge, worth roughly one free skilled professional), and start (cash vs strings vs inherited problems). This section also defines the owner as a person (personal cash, credit, guarantees, draws, the owner's own labor), sandbox and goal scenarios, every difficulty knob, the reputation score, the net worth used for scoring (player-visible marks only), the losing conditions with the end-of-run report, and the first ten turns. Liquidation ends a run; from P4 an eligible company may instead file a Chapter 11 Subchapter V reorganization, which keeps the run alive at a steep price (crashed credit, 3–5 years of plan payments, an investor who turns hostile, and no gold medal in a goal scenario).

### 1.1 Vision and design pillars

**Vision.** Running a real small mining company. Margins are thin, the capital bets are big, and nobody knows exactly what is in the ground. Cash flow can kill a company that is profitable on paper. The player never drives a machine. The game is the decisions: where to dig, what to buy, whom to hire, how to pay for it, when to sell the gold.

| # | Pillar | Mechanic that delivers it (owner §) |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | **You never know what's in the ground.** | Hidden per-block truth (§3). Samples are random draws with nugget effect (§3, §4). Estimates are P10/P50/P90 bands that tighten only when you spend money and time (§4). Seller honesty types (§3). Scoring never uses hidden truth (1.13). |
| P2 | **Cash flow kills profitable companies.** | The season front-loads costs in spring and delivers gold in summer and fall, while debt service, insurance, and salaried staff run all year (§11). Payment priority, the insolvency ladder, and the 13-week forecast (§11). Owner living costs and guarantees put the owner's own money at stake (1.9). |
| P3 | **The season is the clock.** | Breakup and freeze-up are rolled per district per year with a visible forecast range (1.4). Off-season preparation sets in-season output: ground, permits, iron, crew, money. Weekly weather moves water, thaw, hours, and fire closures (1.5). Winter-trail mobilization windows (1.4.5). |
| P4 | **Every bottleneck is visible and every number explains itself.** | The capacity chain shows idle-time attribution (§7). `CalcNode` drill-down on every number (§2.8). The week report and run-to-next-decision summaries (§2.7, §13). |
| P5 | **Real trade-offs, no dominant strategy.** | Buy vs lease vs stake (§5); new vs used vs rent (§9); cash vs debt vs investor (1.8, §11); owner labor vs hiring (1.9); entity choice (1.6). Equal-value background edges (1.7). The simulator's strategy-dominance matrix (§2.12) and background-parity test (1.22). |

**Non-goals.** No real-time play, no 3D, no driving or digging minigame. There is no "reveal the truth" item, though the run's end report does show the truth. Prices are not hand-set by designers: they move by formula.

### 1.2 Core loop and annual rhythm

**Weekly loop.**
1. **Review:** dashboard, inbox, alerts, last week's report, season clock.
2. **Decide:** zero or more actions. Most resolve immediately; time-taking actions create pending records (§2.2).
3. **Advance:** `advanceWeek`, or run-to-next-decision through quiet weeks (§2.7).
4. **Read the result:** production, bottleneck, costs, cash, and news, all drillable.

Most weeks take 1–3 decisions. Off-season weeks with nothing pending are skipped by run-to-next-decision.

**Annual rhythm** (northern P1 district; week = §1.3 calendar):

| Weeks | Phase (typical) | What dominates |
|---|---|---|
| 1–13 (Jan–Mar) | winter | Buy or lease ground. Records review and winter drilling (§4). Winter auctions (§9). Line up money (§11). File notices and plans for summer (§6). Hire for spring (§8). Shop rebuilds. **Winter-trail mobilization closes about week 13.** |
| 14–19 (Apr–mid May) | winter → breakup | Crew arrival, training, camp setup. Spring outflows begin (fuel fill, camp, deposits). Seasonal roads close for breakup. |
| 20–26 (late May–Jun) | operating (start) | Stripping and first sluicing. High stream flow limits in-stream work. Interior fire season peaks (June–July). **The cash low point usually comes in June.** |
| 27–37 (Jul–mid Sep) | operating (peak) | Cleanups every 1–3 weeks; sell or hold gold. **Claim maintenance fee / waiver filing due week 35 (Sept 1).** Strip ahead for next year. |
| 38–44 (late Sep–Oct) | operating → freeze-up | Freeze-up watch. Final cleanup. Keep the plant running into freeze-up at falling capacity, or winterize. Demobilize. Layoffs vs retainers. |
| 45–52 (Nov–Dec) | winter | Season P&L. Bonuses. Year-end tax moves (§11). Insurance renewal (week 49). **Waiver affidavit due week 52 (Dec 30).** Plan next year. |

The arid district runs on a different rhythm. October–April is prime season. June–September is a low season, not a closed one: day-shift hours fall with heat (about ×0.65 in July), Stage-1/Stage-2-like fire restrictions bite in the dry pre-monsoon weeks, and monsoon storms (weeks ~27–38) flood washes and close seasonal roads. Measured over 4,000 simulated years, a day-shift-only plan loses ≈ 6 effective weeks a year, almost all of them June–September (1.5.6). Arid water comes from springs, wells and trucks, not creeks, so its constraint is the cost of water all year rather than a seasonal flow shape (§3, §7). A night shift recovers most of the heat loss at the price of lighting fuel, a wage premium and higher injury odds (§7/§8). The federal calendar deadlines are the same. The company's own annual dates follow its climate: §11's annual DSCR covenant test and revolver clean-up close the season year at week 26 instead of 52 when most of its yards are washed on arid ground (D-11.62), and a seller-carry note on an arid claim pays in week 18 instead of 44 (§5 D-5.56).

**What a player does: four months on the northern creek** (a year-2 company holding one producing claim):
- **January (weeks 1–5).** The year's season forecast lands, e.g. "Breakup wk 18–20, freeze-up wk 40–44". The investor wants an annual plan, if there is one. The player reviews last season's per-claim P&L and cost per ounce, then bids on a used 40t truck at a winter auction (last summer's haul bottleneck), pays for a records review of an adjacent listing, starts a frozen-ground auger program on the bench (§4), asks the bank for a seasonal line (§11), books winter-trail mobilization for week 9 (the trail closes about week 13), and rebuilds the dozer undercarriage while shop labor is idle. Cash falls every week: no gold, but debt service runs.
- **May (weeks 18–22).** Breakup is revealed (say week 19). The seasonal road closes for four to six weeks around it. The crew arrives and does MSHA training (§6/§8). Camp opens, the fuel tanks fill, start-up work and reduced-rate stripping run during breakup (§7), and the first operating week (21) starts washing. High flow (`streamFlowFactor` ≈ 1.5–2.2) delays in-stream work. The 13-week forecast shows the cash trough in mid-June. The player either draws the line or delays the second plant.
- **August (weeks 31–35).** Peak production: 6 days × 11 h, with cleanups every 2 weeks. Each cleanup is a decision: local buyer now, or ship to the refinery and wait. The week-35 claim fee must be paid (or the waiver filed). Interior fire season has passed its June–July peak, but a late fire on the highway corridor can still close the road (§12). The freeze-up forecast narrows (update at week 35). The player strips next year's cut ahead so it thaws and drains before next season.
- **October (weeks 40–44).** Freeze-up comes in week 41. The plant may keep running into freeze-up at §7's falling freeze-up capacity, and from P3 each cold week risks freeze damage to pumps and screens (§7/§9). Winterizing forces the final cleanup. Then the player lays off hourly crew or pays retainers to the two best, pays season bonuses, pays down the line, and books the off-season rebuild list.

### 1.3 Time and calendar

The calendar is fixed: 52 weeks and 365 days, with no leap days. Week *w* covers day-of-year `7(w−1)+1 … 7w`. Week 52 also absorbs Dec 31.

```
turn                 : integer ≥ 0 (absolute week index; turn 0 = year 1 week 1)
year                 = floor(turn / 52) + 1
week                 = (turn mod 52) + 1                                    // 1..52
displayYear          = game.startCalendarYear + year − 1                    // default 2027
doy(month, day)      = cumDays[month] + day                                  // cumDays = [0,31,59,90,120,151,181,212,243,273,304,334]
weekOf(month, day)   = min(52, floor((doy − 1) / 7) + 1)
weekRange(w)         = [doy 7(w−1)+1, w < 52 ? 7w : 365]                     // shown as "Wk 35 · Aug 27–Sep 2, 2027"
weekToDateRange(w)   = { start: dateOf(7(w−1)+1), end: dateOf(w < 52 ? 7w : 365) }          // no year: every year has the same dates
turnDate(t, y0)      = { turn t, year, week, displayYear (y0 = startCalendarYear), start, end }   // §13's label helper
monthOfWeek(w)       = month containing doy 7(w−1)+4                         // the week's middle day; CLIMATOLOGY ONLY (1.5)
reportingMonth(w)    = month containing doy 7(w−1)+1                         // the week's first day; §11 periods and §13 reports
quarter(w)           = ceil(w / 13)                                          // quarter-end weeks 13, 26, 39, 52
monthEndWeeks        = [5, 9, 13, 18, 22, 26, 31, 35, 39, 44, 48, 52]        // week containing each month's last day
```

- **Two month mappings, on purpose.** `reportingMonth` partitions the year exactly as `monthEndWeeks` does (the week containing a month's last day always starts in that month), so §11's months and §13's period selector agree (§13 D-13.18). `monthOfWeek` uses the middle day so that climatology rows switch at the week whose weather is mostly in the new month. Week 5 (Jan 29–Feb 4) reports in January but draws February weather. Nothing else may use `monthOfWeek`.
- **Deadlines.** A rule dated D is due in `weekOf(D)` and resolves in that week's pipeline. The player must act before advancing past that week. There are no weekdays and no weekend shifts. Examples: Sept 1 → week 35, Nov 30 → 48, Dec 30/31 → 52, Apr 1 → 13, Apr 30 → 18. (§2.4 and §6 use this mapping.)
- **Fiscal year = calendar year** for every entity type. Monthly cadences (§11 statements, covenant tests, rent) fire in `monthEndWeeks`. Quarterly cadences fire in weeks 13/26/39/52.
- **Worked example.** Turn 60 → year 2, week 9 → "Wk 9 · Feb 26–Mar 4, 2028". It is month-end for February.

**Key calendar dates** (`data/calendar.ts`; owners resolve them, this table only fixes the week):

| Date | Week | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 15 | 3 | §11 individual Q4 estimated tax |
| ≈ Feb 10 | 6 | §6 discharge/monitoring annual reports |
| Apr 1 | 13 | §6 fees and bond renewals; §1 annual entity fees (`exp.ga`) |
| Apr 15 | 15 | §11 returns and Q1 estimates |
| Apr 30 | 18 | §6 filings; §11 annual-statement covenant |
| Jun 15 | 24 | §11 Q2 estimates |
| Sep 1 | 35 | §6 claim maintenance fee / waiver election |
| Sep 15 | 37 | §11 Q3 estimates |
| Oct 31 | 44 | §6 arid county intent-to-hold |
| Nov 30 | 48 | §6 (AK-style labor and rental, P6) |
| Dec 3–9 | 49 | §11 insurance renewal |
| Dec 15 | 50 | §11 corporate Q4 estimate |
| Dec 30/31 | 52 | §6 waiver affidavit; §1 investor royalty minimum; year close |

### 1.4 Climate templates and season generation

#### 1.4.1 Templates

Each region template (§3) names a `climateTemplateId` and a `fireRestrictionRegime`.

| Template | Phase | Models | Freezing season? | Restriction regime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `northernInterior` | P1 | Fortymile / Circle, interior Alaska BLM ground | yes | `none` (wildfire events only) |
| `aridDesert` | P1 | Nevada low desert (some rows use Arizona normals; see Jurisdictions below) | no | `stage` (BLM Stage 1/2-like) |
| `northernYukon` | P6 | Klondike | yes | `none` |
| `temperateMountain` | P6 | Western mountains (Idaho / Montana / Oregon normals; the state is chosen with its P6 overlay, D-6.56) | yes (snow closes access) | `ifpl` (USFS IFPL-like) |

§3's region templates map onto these: `northernFederal` (P1) and `alaskaState` (P6) → `northernInterior`; `aridFederal` (P1) → `aridDesert`; `yukon` (P6) → `northernYukon`; `temperateFederal` (P6) → `temperateMountain`. `northernYukon` uses the `northernInterior` precipitation rows and fire factors.

**Jurisdictions** (owner ruling 2026-10-05). Districts stay fictional but sit in real jurisdictions, and §6 maps each one's real agencies (D-6.1): the northern federal district and the Alaska-style regime lie in Alaska, the arid federal district in Nevada, and the Yukon-style regime in Yukon. The `aridDesert` climate rows also draw on Arizona low-desert normals and monsoon dates (1.25, R2), which the southern Nevada desert shares in weaker form.

#### 1.4.2 Season phases

`SeasonPhase = 'winter' | 'breakup' | 'operating' | 'freezeup'`, per district per week.

| Phase | Northern / temperate meaning | What is possible |
|---|---|---|
| `winter` | Frozen; snow; ice-bound water | No wet processing. Frozen-ground stripping only with §7's `winterOps` (P3; deepCold weeks 0). Drilling on frozen ground (§4). Winter-trail mobilization (1.4.5). Shop rebuilds. Office work. |
| `breakup` | Thaw, mud, peak runoff, road weight limits | Site prep, start-up, crew arrival and training, camp setup; strip and dig at §7's reduced breakup rate (`ops.breakupWorkMult`). No hauling on seasonal roads. No wet processing (flows too high and turbid). |
| `operating` | Ground workable, water liquid | Everything. Shoulder weeks are slower through §7's cold-water recovery penalty and weather hours (1.5.6). |
| `freezeup` | Sustained freezing | Final cleanup, winterize, demobilize. The plant may keep running at §7's falling `ops.freezeupPlantMult` (P1 flat 0.6), with freeze-damage rolls in cold weeks from P3. Winterizing forces the final cleanup; P1 winterizes automatically at the first winter week (§7 7.12). |

Arid districts are `operating` every week. Their constraints come from weather (heat, water, fire, storms), not phases.

#### 1.4.3 Annual roll (pipeline step 1, week 1, each district)

```
stream: rng(seed, 'season', year, districtId)
draw order (every template draws all eight, in this order, so adding a template never shifts another's draws):
        zB, zF, ε, A_year, n1, n2, n3, n4
zB, zF  ~ N(0,1)                                  // breakup and freeze-up anomalies (also drive spring/fall temperature, 1.5.2)
W_year  = 0.4·W_{year−1} + sqrt(1 − 0.16)·ε       // wetness anomaly, ε ~ N(0,1); W_0 ~ N(0,1); droughts cluster across years
A_year  ~ N(0,1)                                  // arid summer heat anomaly (unused by freezing templates)

Freezing templates (k = template params, table below; s = game.season.sigmaMult by difficulty):
breakupWeek        = clamp(round(k.breakupMean + s·k.breakupSd·zB), k.breakupMin, k.breakupMax)
breakupDurWeeks    = clamp(round(k.breakupDurMean + k.breakupDurSd·n1), 1, 3)          // n1 ~ N(0,1)
operatingStartWeek = breakupWeek + breakupDurWeeks
freezeUpWeek       = clamp(round(k.freezeMean + game.season.freezeUpMeanShift + s·k.freezeSd·zF), k.freezeMin, k.freezeMax)
L                  = freezeUpWeek − operatingStartWeek                                  // operating weeks
if L < k.minOperatingWeeks: freezeUpWeek = operatingStartWeek + k.minOperatingWeeks
if L > k.maxOperatingWeeks: freezeUpWeek = operatingStartWeek + k.maxOperatingWeeks
operatingEndWeek   = freezeUpWeek − 1
freezeDurWeeks     = clamp(round(k.freezeDurMean + k.freezeDurSd·n2), 1, 3)            // winter resumes at freezeUpWeek + freezeDurWeeks

Arid: breakupWeek = freezeUpWeek = null; operatingStartWeek = 1; operatingEndWeek = 52;
      monsoonStartWeek = clamp(round(27 + 1.2·n3), 24, 30); monsoonEndWeek = clamp(round(38 + 1.5·n4), 35, 41)
```

| Param | northernInterior | northernYukon (P6) | temperateMountain (P6) |
|---|---|---|---|
| breakupMean / Sd / min / max | 18.5 / 1.0 / 16 / 22 | 18.3 / 1.0 / 16 / 22 | 19.5 / 1.2 / 16 / 23 |
| breakupDurMean / Sd | 1.4 / 0.6 | 1.4 / 0.6 | 2.0 / 0.6 |
| freezeMean / Sd / min / max | 42.0 / 1.4 / 38 / 46 | 42.5 / 1.4 / 38 / 46 | 45.0 / 1.5 / 41 / 48 |
| min / max operating weeks | 17 / 27 | 17 / 27 | 18 / 29 |
| freezeDurMean / Sd | 2.0 / 0.6 | 2.0 / 0.6 | 1.5 / 0.5 |
| Resulting operating weeks (200k-draw check) | mean 22.0, sd 1.8, P5 19, P95 25 | mean ≈ 22.7 | mean 23.5, P5 20, P95 27 |

**Operating window vs sluicing weeks.** The operating window is the *site season*: heavy iron can work the ground. Full-rate sluicing is shorter. Start-up crew hours on a winterized site (§7), cold-water fine-gold losses in shoulder weeks (§7 `ops.coldWaterExp`), wet-weather hours (P5), and §7's cool-week plant-hours cut (`ops.plantHoursMultByBand`, 1.5.6) together leave about 20 effective sluicing weeks in an average northern year. That matches the reference operation (~20 weeks) and research (Klondike sluicing 18–22, full site season 22–26).

**Difficulty spread** (same 200k-draw check): easy mean 22.5 (P5 20, P95 25); hard mean 21.6 (P5 18, P95 25).

```ts
interface DistrictYearSeason {
  districtId: Id; year: number;
  breakupWeek: number | null; operatingStartWeek: number;      // null for non-freezing climates
  freezeUpWeek: number | null; operatingEndWeek: number; winterResumesWeek: number | null;
  breakupDurWeeks: number | null; freezeDurWeeks: number | null;  // kept so §12 shifts can recompute dependent dates
  monsoonStartWeek: number | null; monsoonEndWeek: number | null;
  z: { breakup: number; freezeUp: number; wetness: number; heat: number };  // hidden drivers
  revealed: { breakup: boolean; operatingStart: boolean; freezeUp: boolean };
  forecast: SeasonForecast;
  shifts: { breakupWeeks: number; freezeUpWeeks: number };     // applied §12 event shifts (1.4.4)
}
interface SeasonForecast {
  asOfWeek: number;
  breakup: { p10: number; p50: number; p90: number } | null;
  freezeUp: { p10: number; p50: number; p90: number } | null;
}
```

#### 1.4.4 Forecasts: what the player sees vs what is true

The true dates are fixed at week 1 and hidden. The player sees a forecast that is re-issued on a schedule. Each issue is a noisy observation of the hidden anomaly.

```
issue weeks / noise variance v (in z² units):
  breakup:  wk 1 → 2.0, wk 9 → 1.0, wk 13 → 0.4, wk 16 → 0.12
  freezeUp: wk 1 → ∞ (climatology), wk 27 → 2.0, wk 35 → 0.6, wk 38 → 0.15
y   = z + sqrt(v)·n,  n ~ N(0,1) from rng(seed, 'season-fc', year, districtId, kind, issueWeek)
m   = y / (1 + v);    sPost = sqrt(v / (1 + v))          // v = ∞ ⇒ m = 0, sPost = 1
μ   = kind = breakup ? k.breakupMean : k.freezeMean + game.season.freezeUpMeanShift      // the same means the roll used
σ   = kind = breakup ? k.breakupSd : k.freezeSd
P50 = round(μ + s·σ·m);  P10/P90 = round(μ + s·σ·(m ∓ 1.2816·sPost)), clamped to [min, max] of that kind
operatingStart forecast = breakup forecast + round(breakupDurMean)
```

- A date is revealed when its phase begins. Forecasts for a revealed date stop.
- Because P10/P90 are rounded to whole weeks, the displayed range covers the truth 85–97% of the time. The UI labels it "likely range". Measured at 200k draws: coverage 0.93 / 0.94 / 0.95 / 0.97 for the four breakup issues (mean widths 2.1 / 1.8 / 1.4 / 0.8 weeks) and 0.93 / 0.91 / 0.92 / 0.95 for the four freeze-up issues (widths 4.0 / 2.9 / 2.2 / 1.3).
- **§12 shifts.** "Early freeze-up" / "mild fall" and "late breakup" / "early breakup" events may add `season.freezeUpShiftWeeks` (−2…+1) or `season.breakupShiftWeeks` (−1…+2) to a date that is not yet revealed. A shift must land at least one week after the event fires. Forecasts do not anticipate shifts; that is the surprise. After a shift §1 recomputes the dependent dates from the stored durations: `operatingStartWeek = breakupWeek + breakupDurWeeks`, `operatingEndWeek = freezeUpWeek − 1`, `winterResumesWeek = freezeUpWeek + freezeDurWeeks`. It then re-applies the min/max operating-week clamps by moving `freezeUpWeek` only (if it is still unrevealed) and recomputes `operatingEndWeek` and `winterResumesWeek` once more.
- **Event windows read the true dates.** §12 fires these events in windows relative to the hidden dates (§12 D-12.9: e.g. early freeze-up in [F−5, F−3]). §1 accepts that. The event announces a change of at least one week, so the small leak reads as a long-range forecast and never reveals the date itself.

**Worked example.** A district rolls zB = +1.3 and zF = −0.8, with a 2-week breakup.
- True dates: breakupWeek = round(18.5 + 1.3) = 20; operatingStart = 22; freezeUp = round(42.0 − 1.12) = 41; L = 19, a short year.
- January breakup forecast (n = −0.4): y = 1.3 − 0.566 = 0.734, m = 0.245, sPost = 0.816. Display: P10 = round(18.5 + 0.245 − 1.046) = 18, P50 = 19, P90 = round(19.79) = 20 → "wk 18–20".
- Week 16 issue (n = +0.5): y = 1.473, m = 1.315, sPost = 0.327 → P10 = round(19.40) = 19, P90 = round(20.23) = 20 → "wk 19–20".

A player who mobilized early pays idle crew for one or two extra weeks.

#### 1.4.5 Access windows

Access types, their cost adders and each district's `roadWinterMaintained` flag belong to §3; the windows below depend on season, so §1 owns them. The engine function is `accessOpen(state, districtId, mode)` for the **current week only**, used by §9 mobilization, §7 fuel and parts delivery, §11 repossession, and §12.

| Access / mode | Open in the current week when |
|---|---|
| `highway` | Always. |
| `seasonalRoad`, winter-maintained (Steese-style) | Not in [breakupWeek − 1, operatingStartWeek + 1]: a 4–6 week breakup closure (`breakupDurWeeks` + 3). |
| `seasonalRoad`, unmaintained (Taylor-style, `roadWinterMaintained = false`) | Only in [operatingStartWeek + 2, freezeUpWeek + 1] of the current year (closed from freeze-up + 2 through next year's breakup closure; R2: Taylor Highway unmaintained mid-Oct to May). |
| `seasonalRoad`, arid | Every week except the week after a `storm` week (washout; `game.access.aridWashoutWeeks` = 1). |
| `winterTrail` (heavy haul) | Phase `winter` AND (week ∈ [`game.access.winterTrailOpenWeek` = 2, breakupWeek − `game.access.winterTrailCloseLeadWeeks` = 5] OR week ≥ this year's freezeUpWeek + `game.access.winterTrailFreezeLagWeeks` = 8). Typical: weeks 2–13 and 50–52. |
| `flyIn` (air) | Always. A week with `precip = storm` delays air freight one week. |
| `flyIn` (barge) | Phase `operating` only. |

Overrides, applied after the table: every mode is closed in a week carrying `EffectModifier` `geology.access.closed` for the district or claim (§3); `access.roadOpen = 0` (§12: washout, wildfire, ice jam) closes `highway`, `seasonalRoad`, `winterTrail` and barge; `access.airOpen = 0` closes air.

**No look-ahead on hidden dates.** Future windows depend on unrevealed breakup and freeze-up weeks, so the player, bots and validators never call `accessOpen` for a future week. Planning uses `accessOutlook(state, districtId, mode, week): 'open' | 'closed' | 'uncertain'`, computed from the current forecast: a window edge that depends on an unrevealed date is evaluated at both that date's P10 and P90, and the answer is `'uncertain'` if they disagree. `phaseOutlook(state, districtId, week)` works the same way for `SeasonPhase`. A booked future action (e.g. §9 "mobilize in week 9 over the trail") is validated against `accessOutlook` when booked (`ACCESS_CLOSED` only when the outlook is `'closed'`) and against `accessOpen` when it executes. If it cannot execute, it slips week by week until the outlook says `'closed'` for the rest of the year, then it fails with a message. A property test scrambles the hidden season drivers and checks that no player-visible selector changes (1.22).

### 1.5 Weekly weather

Weather is drawn in pipeline step 1 for each district, every week:

```ts
interface WeatherWeek {               // pre-agreed shape + two derived fields (Interfaces)
  tempBand: 'deepCold' | 'cold' | 'cool' | 'mild' | 'hot';
  precip: 'dry' | 'normal' | 'wet' | 'storm';
  streamFlowFactor: number;          // multiplier on the claim's baseline surface-water gpm
  fireDanger: number;                // 0..1
  meanTempF: number;                 // weekly mean daily temperature, °F (display & explain)
  fireLevel: 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4;      // restriction level from fireDanger and regime
}
interface WeatherState { tempAnom: number; moistAnom: number; flowAnom: number; drought: number /*0..5*/ }
interface DistrictClimate {                       // one per district; §1-owned
  seasons: Record<number, DistrictYearSeason>;    // keyed by year; current and prior year kept, older dropped
  weather: WeatherWeek;                           // this week's draw (player-visible)
  lastWeather: WeatherWeek | null;                // last week's (arid washout rule, 4-week sff mean for §12)
  sffLast4: number[];                             // ring of the last 4 weekly sff values (§12 drought precondition)
  state: WeatherState;                            // hidden persistence terms
  wetnessPrev: number;                            // W_{year−1} for the annual roll
}
type ClimateSlice = Record<DistrictId, DistrictClimate>;   // requested as top-level state.climate (Interfaces)
```

Streams: weekly `rng(seed, 'weather', turn, districtId)`, drawing εT then εM. The initial state comes from `rng(seed, 'weather-init', districtId)`: anomalies (and `wetnessPrev`) are drawn from their stationary N(0,1); drought starts at 0 (northern/temperate) or 3 (arid); `flowAnom` starts at 0. The player sees this week's weather in the week report and a climatology outlook by month. There is no week-ahead forecast; §7's visible projection uses climatology.

#### 1.5.1 Climatology tables

`Tclim` values are anchored at the week containing the 15th of each month (weeks 3, 7, 11, 15, 20, 24, 28, 33, 37, 42, 46, 50) and interpolated linearly by week, wrapping Dec→Jan. `sdT`, precipitation rows, and F_m are looked up by `monthOfWeek` (no interpolation).

| °F weekly mean (Jan…Dec) | Values | sdT (°F) |
|---|---|---|
| northernInterior | −10, −5, 8, 28, 46, 58, 60, 53, 42, 22, 2, −6 | 12,12,9,7,5,5,5,5,5,7,9,12 |
| northernYukon (P6) | −15, −8, 9, 27, 45, 58, 60, 54, 42, 23, 0, −11 | as northernInterior |
| temperateMountain (P6) | 20, 24, 31, 38, 47, 55, 64, 63, 53, 41, 29, 20 | 6,6,6,5,4,4,4,4,4,5,6,6 |
| aridDesert | 52, 56, 61, 68, 77, 87, 92, 91, 85, 73, 60, 51 | 5,5,5,4,4,4,3,3,4,4,5,5 |

| Precip P(dry/normal/wet/storm) by month | northernInterior | aridDesert | temperateMountain |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | .50/.38/.10/.02 | .60/.25/.11/.04 | .25/.40/.27/.08 |
| Feb | .52/.36/.10/.02 | .60/.25/.11/.04 | .25/.40/.27/.08 |
| Mar | .55/.35/.08/.02 | .65/.23/.09/.03 | .25/.40/.27/.08 |
| Apr | .55/.35/.08/.02 | .78/.16/.05/.01 | .30/.42/.22/.06 |
| May | .45/.40/.12/.03 | .86/.11/.025/.005 | .30/.42/.22/.06 |
| Jun | .33/.42/.19/.06 | .88/.09/.025/.005 | .40/.40/.16/.04 |
| Jul | .25/.42/.25/.08 | monsoon row* | .62/.26/.08/.04 |
| Aug | .25/.40/.27/.08 | monsoon row* | .64/.25/.07/.04 |
| Sep | .30/.43/.21/.06 | monsoon row* | .55/.32/.10/.03 |
| Oct | .40/.42/.15/.03 | .75/.17/.06/.02 | .40/.40/.16/.04 |
| Nov | .45/.40/.13/.02 | .70/.20/.08/.02 | .25/.40/.27/.08 |
| Dec | .48/.38/.12/.02 | .62/.24/.10/.04 | .25/.40/.27/.08 |

\*Arid: inside [monsoonStartWeek, monsoonEndWeek] use `.45/.27/.17/.11`. Outside, July uses the June row and September uses the October row.

| Fire season factor F_m (Jan…Dec) | Values |
|---|---|
| northernInterior / Yukon | 0, 0, 0, .05, .40, .75, .75, .45, .15, 0, 0, 0 |
| aridDesert | .15, .15, .20, .30, .46, .50, .47, .40, .40, .30, .20, .15 |
| temperateMountain | 0, 0, 0, .05, .20, .45, .80, .85, .60, .30, 0, 0 |

Arid F_m is calibrated for the dry pre-monsoon weeks (D-1.30). Over 4,000 simulated years: level 2 in ≈ 40% of June weeks and level 3 in ≈ 40%; level ≥ 3 averages 1.9 weeks/year (P90 4); level 4 never arises from weather alone in the `stage` regime (max fireDanger ≈ 0.80). A full arid shutdown comes only from §12 wildfire closures. The sensitivity is steep: June F_m 0.48 gives 0.8 L3 weeks/year and 0.53 gives 3.2, so tune it in small steps.

#### 1.5.2 Temperature

```
a_t        = 0.55·a_{t−1} + sqrt(1 − 0.55²)·εT                       // weekly persistence
seasonAnom = freezing templates: −zB for weeks 10–24 (late breakup ⇒ cold spring), +zF for weeks 32–46 (late freeze ⇒ warm fall), else 0
             arid: A_year for weeks 18–40, else 0
T (°F)     = Tclim(week) + sdT(week)·(0.8·a_t + 0.6·seasonAnom)
tempBand   = deepCold if T < 0; cold if T < 28; cool if T < 45; mild if T < 80; else hot
phase clamp (freezing templates): operating ⇒ band ≥ cool; winter ⇒ band ≤ cold; breakup ⇒ cold..mild; freezeup ⇒ ≤ cool
            (T is clamped to the band edge so meanTempF agrees with the band)
```

#### 1.5.3 Precipitation

Persistence is added without changing the monthly marginals.

```
m_t    = 0.5·m_{t−1} + sqrt(1 − 0.25)·εM
x_t    = sqrt(1 − 0.4²)·m_t + 0.4·W_year             // marginally N(0,1); lag-1 correlation ≈ 0.58
q      = normCdf(x_t)                                 // dmath
precip = dry if q < pD; normal if q < pD+pN; wet if q < pD+pN+pW; else storm   (row = monthOfWeek, monsoon-aware)
```

#### 1.5.4 Stream flow

```
f_t   = 0.75·f_{t−1} + 0.25·pScore(precip)                  // pScore: dry −1, normal 0, wet +1, storm +2.5
H     = hydrograph (below)
sff   = clamp(H · exp(0.30·f_t + 0.20·W_year) · (precip = storm ? spike[template] : 1), 0.02, 5.0)
spike = northernInterior 1.6, temperate 1.8, arid 4.0 (flash flood in washes)

H northern:  winter 0.05 · breakup 2.2 · operating 0.82 + 0.8·exp(−k/2.5) (k = weeks since operatingStart),
             × (1 − 0.04·max(0, week − 35)) after Sept · freezeup 0.35
H temperate: winter 0.4 · breakup 1.6 · operating 0.65 + 1.5·exp(−((week − 24)/3)²)   (snowmelt peak mid-June; Aug ≈ 0.65)
H arid (Jan…Dec, by monthOfWeek): 1.32, 1.41, 1.32, 0.99, 0.66, 0.52, 0.66, 0.80, 0.80, 0.80, 0.89, 1.13
```

Each H is normalized so the *realized* mean of `sff` over operating weeks is 1.0. The flow, wetness, and storm terms add about 6–10%, so mean H is about 0.94. A 4,000-year simulation gives a realized mean of 0.99 for northern, temperate, and arid. §3's baseline water gpm is therefore an "average operating week". Water sources: `creek` and `ephemeralWash` scale by `sff`. `spring` and `well` scale by `0.9 + 0.1·min(sff, 1.5)`; `none` gives 0 (§3 3.3.4 implements this `sourceScale`).

#### 1.5.5 Fire danger and restriction level

```
D_t        = clamp(0.8·D_{t−1} + dScore(precip), 0, 5)     // dScore: dry +1, normal +0.2, wet −1.5, storm −3; D := 0 when band ≤ cold (snow cover)
heat       = clamp((T − 30) / 35, 0, 1.6)
rainNow    = dry 1.0, normal 0.85, wet 0.45, storm 0.35
fireDanger = clamp(F_m · (0.4 + 0.12·D_t) · heat · rainNow, 0, 1)
fireLevel  = regime 'none' ⇒ 0 always; else 0 if < 0.40, 1 if < 0.60, 2 if < 0.75, 3 if < 0.92, else 4
```

| fireLevel | Real analog | Effect (applied by §7 / §9) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | none | none |
| 1 | IFPL I / fire watch | productive hours ×0.97 (1-hour fire watch after shutdown) |
| 2 | IFPL II "partial hoot owl" / Stage 1 | hours ×0.97. Spark work (field welding, cutting) only at night: field-repair capacity ×0.6. |
| 3 | IFPL III / Stage 2 | Mechanized work only 8 pm–1 pm. A day shift is capped at 8 h (≈ ×0.70 of an 11-h shift). Night shifts are unaffected. |
| 4 | IFPL IV "general shutdown" | All mechanized operations stop (hours 0). |

In northern districts `fireDanger` only drives §12 wildfire events (access closures, evacuation, camp loss).

**Worked example (arid, week 25, Jun 18–24).**
- Temperature: Tclim = 87 + ¼·(92 − 87) = 88.25 °F. With a_t = 0.4 and A_year = 0.5: T = 88.25 + 4·(0.32 + 0.30) = 90.7 → `hot`.
- Precipitation: m_t = −0.2, W_year = −0.5 → x = 0.9165·(−0.2) + 0.4·(−0.5) = −0.383, q = 0.351. That is below 0.88 (June row) → `dry`.
- Drought and fire: D_t = 0.8·4.1 + 1 = 4.28. heat = clamp(60.7/35, 0, 1.6) = 1.6. fireDanger = 0.50 · (0.4 + 0.514) · 1.6 · 1.0 = 0.73 → level 2.
- Hours (suggested §7 curve, 1.5.6): day shift × clamp(1 − 0.03·(90.7 − 80), 0.55, 1) = 0.68; level 2 × 0.97 → 0.66 of a cool-weather day shift.
- Flow: f_t = 0.75·(−0.6) − 0.25 = −0.70 → sff = 0.52 · exp(−0.21 − 0.10) = 0.38. A creek-fed plant has 38% of its baseline water. A well-fed plant has 94%.

#### 1.5.6 What each weather field drives elsewhere

The consuming section owns each constant. "Adopted" rows quote the value that section publishes; the one "requested" row is §1's suggestion, still open with that section (Interfaces).

| Field | Consumer (§) | Hook / key | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tempBand` | §7 thaw of exposed ground (Stefan form) | `ops.thawK[tempBand]` (ft²/week) | deepCold 0, cold 0, cool 1.2, mild 2.0, hot 2.4: ≈ 4–5 cool + 12 mild weeks give 5.4–5.5 ft on stripped gravel (R3: 3–6 ft). Northern hot weeks essentially never occur (July mean 60 °F); `hot` matters for temperate and arid ground. | adopted |
| | §7 recovery in cold water | `ops.coldWaterExp[tempBand]` | fine/ultrafine loss exponent: cold 1.12, cool 1.05 | adopted |
| | §7 freeze-up plant capacity | `ops.freezeupPlantMult` | P1 flat 0.6; P5 by band: cool 0.9, cold 0.5, deepCold 0 | adopted |
| | §7 plant hours, operating phase | `ops.plantHoursMultByBand` | cool 0.80 (night freeze shutdowns), else 1.0; reconciles D-1.3's ≈ 20 sluicing weeks | adopted (P1) |
| | §7/§8 heat (day shift) | `ops.heatDayShiftHoursMult(meanTempF)`; §8 `staff.heatFatiguePerDegF` (0.4 fatigue per °F above 80) and `staff.injury.heatPerDegF` (0.02 heat-illness odds per °F above 80) | `clamp(1 − 0.03·(T − 80), 0.55, 1)` for T ≥ 80 °F (88 °F → 0.76; 92 °F → 0.64); night shift × 0.95 in hot weeks. §7 uses it in `W(t)` in place of a flat `hot` 0.90. | adopted (P1, §7 D-7.29) |
| | §9 cold | `fleet.coldWearMult`, `fleet.coldFuelMult` | deepCold: wear × 1.3, fuel × 1.15; cold: × 1.1 / × 1.05 | adopted |
| | §4 methods | §4 `seasonMult[phase]` per method (0 = not allowed in that phase) | — | §4 |
| `precip` | §7 hours | `ops.weatherHoursMult[precip]` | storm 0.75, wet 0.92, else 1.0 | adopted (P5) |
| | §7 haul and road | `ops.haulCycleMultByPrecip` | wet × 1.10, storm × 1.25 | adopted (P5) |
| | §7 dry washing (arid) | — | runs only on `dry`/`normal` weeks (moisture ≤ 3%, R2) | adopted (P1) |
| | §6 discharge exceedance | `permits.discharge.storm` | dry 0.7, normal 1.0, wet 1.8, storm 4.0 | adopted |
| | §1 access | 1.4.5 | storm delays air freight one week; arid seasonal road washes out the following week | §1 |
| `streamFlowFactor` | §3 / §7 water capacity | §3 `waterAvailableGpm = baseGpm × sourceScale(sff)` (§7 reads it) | 1.5.4 | adopted |
| | §6 complaint detection | low-flow multiplier | 2.0 while sff < 0.7 (water kinds) | adopted |
| | §6 conditions | `noInStreamWork` while sff > `permits.highFlowSff` | 1.6 | requested |
| | §12 preconditions | flood: storm AND sff > `events.flood.sffThreshold` (2.5) · drought: mean of `sffLast4` < 0.5 | — | adopted |
| `fireDanger` / `fireLevel` | §7 hours, §9 field repair | `ops.fireLevelHoursMult`, `fleet.fieldRepairMultByFireLevel` | the 1.5.5 table (L1–L2 × 0.97; L2 field repair × 0.6; L3 day shift ≤ 8 h; L4 = 0) | adopted (P1) |
| | §12 wildfire | P(event) = k_tpl · fireDanger² when fireDanger > 0.3 | §12 owns k | adopted |

**Composite helper.** `weatherHoursMult(state, districtId, shift: 'day' | 'night')` = §7's precipitation factor × the heat factor for that shift × the fire-level factor. §12's competitors use it for their output; §7 may call it instead of composing the keys itself.

**Expected active weeks.** `expectedActiveWeeks(state, districtId, year)` (used by §6 to spread annual inspection rates): freezing templates → the current forecast P50 freeze-up minus P50 operating start (true values once revealed); `aridDesert` → `game.season.expectedActiveWeeks.aridDesert` = 46 (52 minus the measured ≈ 6 heat/fire/storm weeks).

**P1 note.** §7 ships heat and fire-level hours, the cool-week plant cut and the dry-washer rule in P1 with water and thaw (§7 D-7.29, at §1's request D-1.25). Precipitation hours (`ops.weatherHoursMult`) and haul-by-precipitation ship in P5. So in P1 an arid day-shift plan loses ≈ 5.0 effective weeks a year to heat and fire, and ≈ 5.9 from P5 once wet and stormy weeks also cost hours (4,000-year simulation; heat 4.5, fire 0.9 and wet/storm 0.9 measured one at a time, which overlap), concentrated in June–September at ≈ 0.70 of winter output. That gives the arid district a real low season and a day-versus-night shift decision from P1. For comparison: with precipitation hours alone it would lose ≈ 0.9 weeks and nothing but water would make summer differ from winter; a flat heat factor (0.85) with the earlier fire factors gave ≈ 4.1. `game.season.expectedActiveWeeks.aridDesert` (46) uses the full-rules loss.

### 1.6 Company setup and entity type

**Setup wizard order:** mode/scenario → difficulty → company and owner names → entity → background → start (plus Backed terms) → world settings (seed, start year, opening spot, districts) → tutorial on/off. Setup is `newGame(setup, seed)`, not an action.

```ts
interface NewGameSetup {
  companyName: string; ownerName: string;                 // 1–40 chars each
  entity: EntityType; background: OwnerBackground; start: StartType;
  backedTerms: 'equity' | 'royalty' | null;               // required iff start = 'backed'
  mode: 'sandbox' | 'scenario'; scenarioId: ScenarioId | null;
  difficulty: Difficulty;
  world: { startCalendarYear: number; districtTemplates: RegionTemplateId[]; openingSpotUsdPerFineOz: number | null };
  tutorial: boolean;
}
// validation (validateSetup returns every issue with its field; newGame throws SetupError with them; D-1.63):
//   NAME_EMPTY, NAME_TOO_LONG (trimmed names, NAME_MAX_LENGTH = 40), BACKED_TERMS_REQUIRED, BACKED_TERMS_UNEXPECTED (terms
//   without a Backed start), ENTITY_NOT_ALLOWED (soleProp + backed equity; scenario restrictions), SCENARIO_UNKNOWN (also a
//   sandbox setup with a non-null scenarioId), DISTRICT_TEMPLATE_NOT_IN_PHASE, INHERITOR_NEEDS_NORTHERN (inheritor without a
//   northernFederal district), START_NOT_IN_PHASE (a start the build cannot run; a P0 build runs only the Bootstrapper),
//   START_YEAR_INVALID (not an integer in 1900–2500), OPENING_SPOT_INVALID (neither null nor a positive finite number)
// world defaults: P1–P5 districtTemplates = ['northernFederal', 'aridFederal']; P6 adds up to 4 more (templates may repeat).
//   §3's generateWorld receives districtCount = districtTemplates.length and templateIds = districtTemplates.
//   openingSpotUsdPerFineOz null ⇒ market.openingSpotUsdPerFineOz (4,200); otherwise it replaces that key (also §10's referenceSpot),
//   and startCalendarYear replaces game.startCalendarYear, both in §2.10's setup layer of tuning resolution (D-2.36).
```

Entity tax and liability mechanics belong to §11; this table summarizes them.

| | Sole proprietorship | LLC (single-member, pass-through) | Corporation (C-corp) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Formation (one-time) | $0 (`game.entity.soleProp.formationUsd`) | $1,200 (state filing ≈ $250 + operating agreement) | $2,500 (filing + bylaws + attorney) |
| Annual entity fees (`exp.ga`, week 13) | $0 | $550 (state annual report + registered agent) | $850 (annual report, registered agent, franchise) |
| Liability shield | **None.** Every company debt, judgment, fine, and reclamation obligation reaches personal cash. | Yes, except: guaranteed debts, payroll trust-fund taxes (TFRP, always personal), unpaid wages after the bankruptcy wage priority (the owner with operational control is an FLSA "employer", §11 D-11.23), and owner draws taken within `game.drawClawbackWeeks` = 13 weeks before the bankruptcy petition (clawed back at liquidation; the look-back runs from the first filing, so a reorganization that converts looks back from its own filing date, D-1.59) | As LLC |
| Income tax (§11 11.18) | Profit taxed to the owner at the 2026 single-filer brackets (10–37%) + SE tax 15.3% to the wage base (2.9% above), less the 20% QBI deduction (`finance.tax.qbiRate`). At typical profits ($100–250k) the marginal rate is 22–32% plus SE tax (D-11.18). Paid from the owner book, normally through automatic tax distributions. Draws are not deductible. | Same as sole proprietor (disregarded entity). No S-election in v1. | 21% federal + state per §11's tax jurisdiction at company level. Owner salary is a deductible wage (payroll taxes). Distributions are taxed again as dividends (`finance.tax.dividendRate` 15%). |
| Lender view (§11) | The owner *is* the borrower. Personal credit is the only score. No guarantee records; full recourse. **Edge:** for the first 104 weeks (`finance.credit.solePropOwnerFileWeeks`) the owner's personal file stands in for the company's missing payment history: U's paydex term uses the owner's score (§11 11.5, D-11.52). A Bootstrapper sole prop scores U ≈ 168 (C, near B) at week 3, against ≈ 153 (C) for the same owner as an LLC. | Company file starts thin. Every loan needs a full personal guarantee (PG) until ≥ 24 months of clean history and company tier ≥ B. After that, equipment lenders may accept a limited PG (50%); banks keep a full PG. | As LLC |
| Equity investors | Not possible; must convert first | Yes (membership units) | Yes (shares; cleanest cap table for §11 equity partners) |
| At liquidation (Chapter 7; game over) | Personal cash above `game.personalBankruptcyExemptionUsd` = $25,000 (cash wildcard; no home is modeled) is seized. Bankruptcy mark on the owner's file (§11 11.5: base 240 × 0.7–1.0 by the prior score, i.e. −168 to −240; R5 −130 to −240). | Guaranteed deficiencies are charged to personal cash. Unguaranteed debt dies with the company. | As LLC |
| In reorganization (Chapter 11 Subchapter V, P4+; mechanics §11) | The owner files as an individual in business (Subchapter V is open to individuals as well as companies), so one case covers the business and the owner's personal debts. Personal cash above the exemption counts toward the creditors' best-interest test, and the owner lives on the living allowance (1.9). Bankruptcy mark on the owner's file. | The company files and the owner keeps the equity. Guarantees stay enforceable: at confirmation the owner gets a demand for what the plan will not pay, unless the owner joins the filing as guarantor (`guarantorFiles`, §11), which puts the guarantees and the owner's personal debts into the plan and the owner's personal cash into the best-interest test. TFRP and unpaid wages stay personal. The company file takes a bankruptcy mark; the owner's file takes §11's lighter affiliate mark, or the full mark as a filing guarantor. | As LLC |

The $50 business and mining license is a §6 permit (`st.businessLicense`, every entity, from P2), not an entity fee. Tax-return preparation is billed by §11 (`finance.tax.entityReturnPrepUsd`, 11.18), not as an entity fee.

Trade-offs: **sole prop** is free and simple (no formation cost, no annual fees, no entity filings; the owner's Schedule C is the only return) and borrows cheaper early: for two years its company file carries the owner's payment history (≈ +15 U, half a tier; above). But one bad season can take the owner's savings, and it never escapes full recourse. **LLC**: $1,200 plus about $550/yr buys a shield, but early lenders demand PGs anyway, so it matters most against fines, judgments, unsecured vendors, and in the distress ladder, where demands on personal cash drain the savings that could rescue the company. **C-corp**: retained profit taxed at 21% (good for reinvesting), but cash paid to the owner is taxed twice and admin costs are highest. The sole prop is the cheap-credit, high-exposure choice (D-1.36); the simulator holds its cautious-bot survival within 5 pp of the LLC's (1.22).

Conversions (`company/convertEntity`) are one-way: soleProp→LLC, soleProp→corp, LLC→corp. Each costs the formation fee and takes `game.entityConversionWeeks` = 4 weeks. Tax treatment switches at the next week 1. Pre-conversion debts stay personal.

### 1.7 Owner backgrounds

Each background gives **exactly one edge**: the owner counts as a skilled professional in one domain, at no wage. A free skilled hire is worth roughly the same everywhere ($90–150k/yr), but each one pulls the company toward a different strategy. Field edges (operator, mechanic) use the owner's single labor assignment (1.9). Desk edges (geologist, banker, landman) run mostly on desk days, so those owners can also serve as a mediocre foreman (skill 40) on top of their edge. That is why field edges get higher skill (85) than desk edges (geologist 75 as §4 calibrated it, landman 80). On a crew of three or fewer, §8's small-crew rule lets a claim run with no foreman at all (efficiency 0.92, one shift and one plant line only, incident odds × 1.15), so a desk owner may also stay in the office there (1.9, 1.21).

| Background | The one edge | Tuning keys (default) | Implements | P1 stub | Strategy it favors | Est. value/yr (reference op) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Operator** | When assigned foreman or operator on a claim, the owner works at ops skill 85. Every other background's owner works at 40. | `staff.ownerOpsSkillByBackground` = {operator 85, others 40} | §8 owner record and skill curves; §7 foreman efficiency; §9 wear | Works in P1 as specified | Lean, early production with a small crew; no foreman hire | $110–150k: replaces a $125k foreman wherever one is required (crews above three, a second shift or a second plant line), or ≈ +6–7% throughput on a small crew (F 0.9775 against 0.91 for a skill-40 owner-foreman or 0.92 with no foreman) |
| **Mechanic** | The owner is a skill-85 heavy-duty mechanic. Inspects any listed or owned machine free (1 day; ≤ 2/week; any assignment). When assigned to `shop`, adds 50 shop labor-hours/week in its mode: one claim's site shop, or (P3+) the district pool, based at the district yard, that serves every road-access claim in the district at §9's travel overhead and response delay. | `staff.ownerMechanicSkill` 85, `staff.ownerShopHoursPerWeek` 50, `staff.ownerInspectionsPerWeek` 2 | §8, §9 inspection accuracy and repair quality | Owner in `shop` (site mode): flat maintenance $/hr ×`fleet.p1OwnerShopMaintMult` 0.70 on the machines of the claim the assignment names (§9 9.14) | Cheap used and auction iron, kept running | $100–150k: a mechanic at ~2,300 h × $45 × 1.22, plus avoided lemons |
| **Geologist** | The owner is a skill-75 geologist (§4 D-4.26): supervises one prospecting or drilling program as `fieldGeologist` in place of a hired geologist (drilling requires one); records reviews at reviewer quality 0.9 (vs 0.6 for other owners); seller-data reviews and verification without a consultant, at §4's tell `skillMult` 1.15 (a salted-signature tell is caught at 0.65 × 1.15 ≈ 0.75); results reports always carry recommendations. When assigned foreman or operator on claim C, the owner also supervises one program on C without a separate assignment (1.9). The estimator itself is the same for everyone (§4). | `geology.ownerGeologistSkill` 75 (§4 owns the value) | §4 programs, records, audits; §8 | None needed: §4 ships the edge in P1 (pans, records, pits, recommendations) | Cheap unproven ground and staking; catching seller fraud | $80–150k, lumpy: replaces a $105k geologist and consultant days; one avoided bad claim pays for years |
| **Banker** | Lenders underwrite the company **one credit tier better** than its score implies, for pricing, limits, approvals, and seasonal structures: +35 U points on every lender's appetite score and on the lender-neutral `creditTier`. As part of the same access-to-capital edge, the bank's history gate needs one profitable fiscal year instead of two (§11 11.6). | `finance.bankerCreditTierBonus` 1 × `finance.tierWidthPoints` 35 (= +35 U points, one tier); `finance.bank.bankerMinProfitableYears` 1 (vs `minProfitableYears` 2); §11 owns all three values (D-11.58) | §11 11.5–11.6 lender appetite, pricing and the bank gate | At setup, a $150k 60-month term loan at prime + 2.0% (9.0%, $3,113.75/mo) with PG, reusing P1's fixed-loan code | Leverage: cheaper equipment debt from year 1 and a bank line and seasonal structures a year earlier, not hard money | $70–140k: 4–6 points of spread on $0.6–1.0M plus a bank line one season sooner |
| **Landman** | The owner is a skill-80 land specialist (desk). The skill-80 figure drives §5 only: negotiation logit, hint band and title diligence (`landSkill`). Permit applications the owner prepares use §6's owner-prep keys instead of §8's hired-specialist curve (which would give 0.85 / 0.85 at skill 80), because the owner prepares on desk days: quality 0.65 (vs 0.40) and speed 1.1 (vs 1.6). | `staff.ownerLandSpecialistSkill` 80; `permits.ownerPrepQuality.landman` 0.65, `permits.ownerPrepSpeed.landman` 1.1 (§6 values) | §5 5.11; §6 6.5 (preparer quality and speed) | Purchase prices ×`land.p1LandmanPriceMult` 0.925; lease royalties −`land.p1LandmanRoyaltyPointsOff` 1.0 point (floor 1%) until P5 | Better terms and faster permits; permitted ground sooner | $80–150k: replaces a $90k specialist; −1 royalty point ≈ $19k/yr; one season gained on a plan |

Rules: owner-role effects **do not stack** with a hired employee in the same role (the higher skill applies), but the mechanic's shop hours add to capacity. The owner never quits and has no morale, but takes fatigue and injury rolls (§8) in field assignments. Desk edges spend the owner's desk days (1.9 owner time). **Balance gate:** the `cautious` bot's 2-season going-concern survival (S2, BALANCE §5.2) by background must sit within ±5 pp of the mean (1.22; BALANCE O-07 allows ±7 pp in P1–P2 while the mechanic and banker edges run on stubs). §4 adds its own check: a geologist start must not exceed 1.15× the other backgrounds' median net worth. **Simulator-only neutral owner:** the harness's `--background none` (§2.12, D-2.27) is an owner with every 1.7 edge at its non-background value (ops skill 40, no mechanic, geologist, banker or landman edge, no P1 stub). BALANCE's core matrix uses it so start and bot comparisons carry no edge. It is a simulator-only setup value (`background: 'none'`), never offered in the setup wizard.

### 1.8 Start types

| | Bootstrapper | Backed (equity) | Backed (royalty) | Inheritor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Company cash | $400,000 (`game.start.bootstrapper.companyCashUsd`) | $1,500,000 | $1,100,000 | $300,000 (`game.start.inheritor.companyCashUsd`) |
| Of which owner capital / investor money | $400k / — | $200k / $1.3M | $200k / $0.9M | estate account |
| Personal cash | $120,000 (`game.start.bootstrapper.personalCashUsd`) | $50,000 | $50,000 | $40,000 |
| Personal credit score (§11 scale 300–850; R5 tiers A ≥ 720, B 680–719) | 760 | 720 | 720 | 680 |
| Assets | none | none | none | family claims (two blocks pre-stripped), worn fleet, camp (below) |
| Debts | none | none | none | $320,000 estate note (seasonal, Jun–Nov) + $12,000 fuel AP |
| Entity constraint | any | LLC or corp | any | any (LLC/corp: owner must PG the note) |
| Starting reputation / regulator standing (§6) | 45 / 60 | 50 / 60 | 50 / 60 | 55 / 55 |
| Owner net worth at start (1.13) | $520,000 | $250,000 | $250,000 | ≈ $280,000 (P1) / ≈ $238,000 (P2+: + $6k bond − ARO on ≈ 8 open acres) |

Backed company cash is the owner's $200k plus the investor contribution (`game.investor.equityContributionUsd` / `royaltyContributionUsd`). Bootstrapper and Inheritor cash were raised from an earlier $250k and $90k after the preflight model showed both starts dying of first-season liquidity, not geology (D-1.42), and the Inheritor's again from $250k to $300k when the second preflight still put its S2 at 46% (D-1.54). The Inheritor's owner NW is $300k cash + Σ `resaleEstimate` of the inherited fleet (≈ $152k, 1.8.2) + $120k claims at appraisal − $332k debts + $40k personal ≈ $280k.

Difficulty scales company cash (`game.startCompanyCashMult`), personal cash (`game.startPersonalCashMult`), and the Inheritor's note (`game.inheritorDebtMult`). For Backed starts the company-cash multiplier scales the owner's capital and the investor's contribution alike, and the investor's terms (40%, 8%, 10% / 2.0× / 3%) do not change. The royalty payback threshold (2.0× the contribution) and the minimum ($100k × the multiplier) follow the scaled contribution. The Inheritor's fleet, claims and fuel AP are not scaled. The cash multipliers are deliberately narrow (1.25 / 1.0 / 0.85; D-1.43): difficulty works mainly through information honesty, lender patience and events.

**Opening capital** (D-1.64). `newGame` posts the start's cash through the ledger, so cash has an explanation from turn 0: company cash × `game.startCompanyCashMult` as the owner's capital contribution (`cash.operating` / `eq.ownerCapital`, company book), and personal cash × `game.startPersonalCashMult` in the owner book (`own.cash` / `own.equity`). A Bootstrapper's scoring net worth therefore starts at the table's $520,000 ($400,000 + $120,000 on standard). A P0 build implements only the Bootstrapper start (`START_NOT_IN_PHASE` for the others, 1.6); the other starts' postings (investor money, the estate note, inherited assets) arrive with the systems that hold them.

Trade-offs: **Bootstrapper** has full control and good credit but cash for only a modest fleet and one frozen first season; the game is choosing ground well and growing on PG-backed equipment debt (P4). **Backed** fields a reference-size operation (equity) or nearly one (royalty) from day one, but someone else takes a cut, and the equity investor also has opinions. **Inheritor** has iron on site, two blocks the family stripped ahead, and ground with history, but ≈ $62k/yr of debt service falls due in every operating season, the ground's quality is unknown, and the machines are tired.

#### 1.8.1 Backed: investor terms

The player picks the terms at setup. Royalty money is smaller ($0.9M vs $1.3M) because it comes with full control. Both terms are generous on purpose: the investor is backing the owner, not proven ground. The reference operation makes ≈ 430 fine oz in an established season (≈ 350 in a first frozen season with nothing stripped ahead; §7 engine, D-1.51), ≈ $1.8M at spot. At 430 oz, 10% is worth ≈ $181k/yr, so $0.9M is ≈ 5.0× the expected annual royalty. R5's market rule for investor royalties is 2–4×, and only 1–2× on unproven ground. The investor's return still clears a small-producer hurdle: payback takes ≈ 10 seasons at that output, an IRR of ≈ 17% including the 3% tail over a 20-year mine life. A bigger operation pays it back faster: royalty worth $300k/yr gives ≈ 28%, and $420k/yr ≈ 38%. Investor money is posted to `eq.investor` (equity) or `deferred.revenue.<agreementId>` (royalty), so the owner's starting net worth is $250k either way.

| | Equity | Royalty |
|---|---|---|
| Instrument | $1.3M (`game.investor.equityContributionUsd`) for 40% ownership (`game.investor.equityPct`). Non-participating 1× liquidation preference. 8% cumulative preferred return on $1.3M (`game.investor.prefRate`), accruing from year 2 ($104k/yr). Drag-along right (used by the redemption demand). | $0.9M (`game.investor.royaltyContributionUsd`) for a `ProductionInterest` of kind `investorRoyalty`: 10% of attributable fine oz (after lease royalties and JV owner shares; §5 `level: 'attributable'`), in kind (`game.investor.royaltyRate`), until 2.0× the contribution ($1.8M at spot on delivery) has been delivered (`game.investor.royaltyPaybackMultiple`), then 3% for life (`game.investor.royaltyTailRate`). Settled by §5 at every cleanup on every company claim. Runs with the claims: a sold claim carries it. Matches R5's "10% of gross until 1.5–2.0×, then 2–3% for life". |
| Minimum | Pref accrues if unpaid. Arrears block owner draws above living cost. | From year 2 until payback: `game.investor.royaltyMinimumUsd` = $100,000/yr. A shortfall is a cash top-up due in week 52. |
| Control | Board seat, monthly reporting. Capex or new debt above `game.investor.approvalThresholdUsd` ($100k; R5's example is "any item over ~$50k", raised to keep approvals to the big bets) needs approval: automatic while content, rolled otherwise (stance table and approval flow below). | None, but a lien on the claims secures the minimum. |
| Distributions | Pro rata: an owner draw of D pays the investor D × 0.40/0.60 at the same time. Owner salary up to `game.ownerReasonableSalaryCapUsd` = $150k/yr is not a distribution; salary above the cap is treated as a draw. | n/a |
| Exit | Owner buyout at any time: `BP = 1.10 × claim_a` (waterfall below). | Buyback before payback: `BB = max(1.0 × 0.9M, 2.0 × 0.9M − value delivered to date)`; the 3% tail alone buys back at 3 × trailing-year tail value. |
| Check-ins | Quarterly (weeks 13/26/39/52) plus an annual plan in week 1 | Annual (week 52) |

**One model for every equity holder.** The Backed investor and every equity partner §11 admits later (angel, family office, mining fund, rescue partner; at most `finance.maxEquityPartners` = 2 equity agreements at once) are `InvestorAgreement`s with their own terms. Check-ins, approvals, stance and ouster below apply to each. Royalty-form agreements are liabilities (`deferred.revenue`), not equity.

```
Equity waterfall (pure; used by net worth, buyouts and the end report)
  remaining = max(0, companyNW)                                   // companyNW per 1.13, before investor claims
  for a in equity agreements, most senior first (later money is senior; ties by id):
     pref_a  = a.liquidationPrefMult × a.contributed + a.prefUnpaid
     conv_a  = a.equityPct × max(0, companyNW)
     claim_a = min(remaining, max(pref_a, conv_a))                // non-participating: the greater of preference or conversion
     remaining −= claim_a
  ownerShare = companyNW − Σ_a claim_a                            // ≥ 0 whenever companyNW ≥ 0; equals companyNW if companyNW < 0
  ownerPct   = 1 − Σ_a a.equityPct
Pro-rata distributions: an owner draw D pays each equity holder D × a.equityPct / ownerPct in the same week.

Check-in (quarterly, each equity agreement)
  planYTD   = annualPlanFineOz × profile[quarter]     // northern profile Q1..Q4 = 0, .25, .75, 1.0; arid = .35, .60, .70, 1.0
  ΔS        = sProd + sCash + sDistress + sReturn + 0.1·(60 − S)
  sProd     = planYTD > 0 ? clamp(25·(fineOzYTD / planYTD − 1), −10, +8) : 0
  sCash     = runway ≥ 13 wk ? +3 : runway ≥ 6 ? 0 : −6            // runway = weeks until §11 forecast13 P50 goes negative
  sDistress = missed payroll −12 | loan default notice −8 | missed reorganization plan payment −8
              | in reorganization (case open at any time in the quarter) −6 | covenant breach −4
              | investor requirement missed −4 (monthly report, hedge share) | none +2   (worst of quarter)
  sReturn   = Q4 and year ≥ 2: returnPaidYTD ≥ returnDueYTD ⇒ +5 | partial ⇒ −3 | none ⇒ −8
              returnDueYTD = pref accrued this year (prefRate × contributed, from year 2) + a.distributionExpectation × FCF
              FCF = §11 operating cash flow − capex, year to date (family office only; others have no expectation)
  S0 = 65 (rescue partner 45); plan below floor (year 1: 200, year 2: 450, year 3+: 600 fine oz) ⇒ −5 at submission
  negative terms scaled by game.investor.penaltyMult (difficulty); S is clamped to [0, 100] after each check-in
```

**Approval flow.** An action that needs consent (§9 purchase, §11 `finance/apply`, §5 purchase above an agreement's threshold) fails with `INVESTOR_APPROVAL_REQUIRED`. The player sends `investor/requestApproval { subject: 'capex' | 'debt', amountUsd, ref }`. It resolves at once from each agreement's stance: content grants it; concerned grants it with p = S/100; unhappy grants it with p = max(0, S/100 − 0.2) and halves the threshold (floor $25k); hostile refuses. The draw is `rng(seed,'investor','approval',agreementId,subject,requestIndex)`, where `requestIndex` is the agreement's count of earlier requests on that subject (`approvalRequestCount`). It is keyed by the request, not by `actionSeq` or turn, so reloading a save and re-asking gets the same answer (§2.3; §13 undo rules). A grant is a token for that subject and amount, valid `game.investor.approvalTokenWeeks` = 4 weeks and consumed by the matching action. A refusal blocks new requests on that subject for `game.investor.approvalCooldownWeeks` = 4 weeks, so a denied purchase cannot be re-rolled every week. **Annual plan:** `investor/submitPlan { annualFineOz, capexBudgetUsd }` puts the whole budget through one approval roll at submission (same stream, subject `'plan'`, requestIndex = year). If it is approved, capex items within the remaining budget need no further request that year. If it is refused, items go through requests one by one.

**Paying the return.** The pref accrues weekly from year 2 (`prefRate × contributed / 52`).
